Let $(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on it, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of real-valued $\Sigma$-measurable functions that are integrable under both $P$ and $Q$. The **integral probability metric** induced by $\mathcal F$ is
$$d_{\mathcal F}(P,Q):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\int_S f\,dP-\int_S f\,dQ\right|\in[0,+\infty].$$
It is nonnegative and symmetric, and it may equal $+\infty$; no separation property is asserted for an arbitrary class $\mathcal F$.

u$ be countably additive Borel probability measures on $X$, and fix $x_0\in X$. Let $\Pi_X(\mu,
u)$ be the Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on the product-topology space $X	imes X$ satisfying $\gamma(A	imes X)=\mu(A)$ and $\gamma(X	imes A)=

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space. Write $\mathcal B(X)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of its metric topology. A Borel probability measure on $X$ is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(X)$ with total mass one. For Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $X$, let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the set of Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on $X\times X$, with its product topology and Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A),\qquad \gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A).$$
Define
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the infimum is taken in the extended real line and $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The integrand is nonnegative and Borel: the triangle inequality and symmetry give
$$|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y'),$$
so $(x,y)\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous for the product topology; nonnegativity follows from the metric axioms.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of A measurable function between measurable spaces.

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space, the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then
$\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
(Extended-real-valued measurable functions) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: By [F4] and [F6], every $P_\theta$ is a probability measure. By [F5], $P_\theta(A)=\rho(G_\theta^{-1}(A))$ for every Borel $A\subseteq X$. If $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{A_j}$ is nonnegative simple with disjoint Borel sets, [F7]–[F8] give $\int s\,dP_\theta=\sum_j c_jP_\theta(A_j)=\sum_jc_j\rho(G_\theta^{-1}(A_j))=\int s\circ G_\theta\,d\rho$. For any bounded Borel real $f$, apply [F9] to $f^+$ and $f^-$; their increasing simple approximants are bounded by $\|f\|_\infty$, whose integral is finite under both probability measures. Applying [F10] to the approximants and their compositions gives equality of the positive-part integrals and of the negative-part integrals; [F11] then yields $\int f\,dP_\theta=\int f(G_\theta(z))\,d\rho(z)$.

The zero function belongs to $\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$, so this class is nonempty; it is also symmetric under $f\mapsto-f$, so its supremum of absolute integral differences equals its signed supremum. It is exactly the bounded Borel version of the compact KR test class in [F2]. Hence $V(\theta)=W_1^X(\mu,P_\theta)$ for every $\theta$, with the coupling-cost convention in [F3].

Fix $\theta_0$ and its attaining critic, and choose $r>0$ such that the ball $B(\theta_0,r)$ lies in the envelope neighborhood. Let $E$ be the intersection of its measurable full-measure set with a measurable full-measure set where the composite is Fréchet differentiable. Extend the measurable derivative by zero off $E$. On $E$ its norm is at most $K_{\theta_0}$, by the envelope and the critic's $1$-Lipschitz inequality, so all coordinates are integrable. Write $R(h,z)=H_{\theta_0}(\theta_0+h,z)-H_{\theta_0}(\theta_0,z)-D_\theta H_{\theta_0}(\theta_0,z)[h]$. For $j\ge1$ put $s_j=\min\{r/2,1/j\}$ and let $Q_j(z)$ be zero off $E$ and otherwise the supremum of $|R(q,z)|/\|q\|$ over rational $p$-tuples with $0<\|q\|<s_j$, including zero among the values. The explicit enumeration and [F13] give measurability; the envelope gives $0\le Q_j\le2K_{\theta_0}$, and pointwise Fréchet differentiability gives $Q_j\to0$ on $E$. By [F10], $\int Q_j\,d\rho\to0$. On $E$ the remainder ratio is continuous in nonzero $h$ by the envelope, so rational density [F12] bounds it by $Q_j$ for every real $0<\|h\|<s_j$. Therefore $|\int R(h,z)\,d\rho|/\|h\|\le\int Q_j\,d\rho$ for all such $h$, proving the full Fréchet limit without a sequential-criterion choice step. Thus $\Phi(\theta)=\int f_{\theta_0}\,d\mu-\int H_{\theta_0}(\theta,z)\,d\rho(z)$ has derivative $-\int D_\theta H_{\theta_0}(\theta_0,z)\,d\rho(z)$.

Fix $\theta_0$ and a ball $B(\theta_0,r)\subseteq\Theta$. Put $s_j=\min\{r/2,1/j\}$. On $Z_0$, let $S_j(z)$ be the supremum of $d(G_{\theta_0+q}(z),G_{\theta_0}(z))$ over rational $p$-tuples with $\|q\|<s_j$, and set it to zero off $Z_0$. It is measurable by the assumed distance measurability, [F12] and [F13], is bounded by $D$, and tends pointwise to zero by parameter continuity. Thus [F10] gives $\int S_j\,d\rho\to0$. Parameter continuity and rational density make $S_j$ dominate the same distance for all real increments $\|h\|<s_j$ on $Z_0$. For every critic $f$, step 1.1 and its $1$-Lipschitz property give $|\Delta_{\theta_0+h}(f)-\Delta_{\theta_0}(f)|\le\int S_j\,d\rho$, where $\Delta_\theta(f)=\int f\,d\mu-\int f\,dP_\theta$. The same bound holds for the difference of their absolute values and hence of the two suprema. It follows that $|V(\theta_0+h)-V(\theta_0)|\le\int S_j\,d\rho$ for all $\|h\|<s_j$, proving continuity.

Under the common-neighborhood envelope, the same estimate gives $|\Delta_\theta(f)-\Delta_{\theta'}(f)|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|\int K_{\theta_0}\,d\rho$ for every $f\in\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$ and $\theta,\theta'\in U$. Taking absolute values and then suprema proves the stated local-Lipschitz bound for $V$.

By optimality, $\Phi(\theta_0)=V(\theta_0)$ and $\Phi(\theta)\le V(\theta)$ for every $\theta$. Thus $V-\Phi$ has a local minimum of $0$ at $\theta_0$. Along every direction $v$, differentiability and the two one-sided difference quotients at this minimum give $D(V-\Phi)(\theta_0)[v]=0$; since this holds for every $v$, the derivative of the difference is zero, giving the claimed gradient formula.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space, fix $x_0\in X$, and let $D<\infty$ satisfy $d(x,y)\le D$ for all $x,y\in X$. Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$, let $(Z,\Sigma,\rho)$ be a probability space, and let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open with $p\ge1$. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, let $G_\theta:Z\to X$ be measurable and define its law by $P_\theta(B)=\rho(G_\theta^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq X$. Assume $z\mapsto d(G_\theta(z),G_{\theta'}(z))$ is $\rho$-measurable for every $\theta,\theta'\in\Theta$, and that there is a measurable set $Z_0\subseteq Z$ with $\rho(Z_0)=1$ on which $\theta\mapsto G_\theta(z)$ is continuous. Let $\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$ be the class of bounded Borel functions $f:X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x_0)=0$ and $|f(x)-f(y)|\le d(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$, and set $V(\theta)=d_{\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)}(\mu,P_\theta)$. Then $V(\theta)=W_1^X(\mu,P_\theta)$ and $V$ is continuous on $\Theta$.

Suppose in addition that for every $\theta_0\in\Theta$ there are an open neighborhood $U\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$, a measurable $K_{\theta_0}:Z\to[0,+\infty)$ with $\int K_{\theta_0}\,d\rho<\infty$, and a measurable full-measure set $Z_{\theta_0}\subseteq Z$ such that, for every $z\in Z_{\theta_0}$ and every $\theta,\theta'\in U$,
$$
d(G_\theta(z),G_{\theta'}(z))\le K_{\theta_0}(z)\|\theta-\theta'\|.
$$
Then $V$ is locally Lipschitz, with $|V(\theta)-V(\theta')|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|\int K_{\theta_0}\,d\rho$ for $\theta,\theta'\in U$. At any such $\theta_0$ where $V$ is Fréchet differentiable, if the signed dual supremum at $\theta_0$ is attained by $f_{\theta_0}\in\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$ and $H_{\theta_0}(\theta,z)=f_{\theta_0}(G_\theta(z))$ is Fréchet differentiable in $\theta$ at $\theta_0$ for $\rho$-almost every $z$ with measurable derivative, then
$$
\nabla V(\theta_0)=-\int_Z\nabla_\theta H_{\theta_0}(\theta_0,z)\,d\rho(z).
$$
Here Fréchet differentiability of a scalar function $F$ at $\theta_0$ means there is a linear map $A$ such that $F(\theta_0+h)=F(\theta_0)+A[h]+o(\|h\|)$ as $h\to0$. The attainment and composite-differentiability assumptions are pointwise hypotheses for the gradient formula; compact dual attainment is not asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and locally Lipschitz map $u:U\to\mathbb R^m$ (each point has a neighborhood on which $|u(y)-u(z)|\le L|y-z|$ for some finite $L$, [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), $u$ is Frechet differentiable outside a null subset of $U$. Here Frechet differentiability at $x$ means that a linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ satisfies $u(x+h)=u(x)+Ah+o(|h|)$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ (Sigma-algebras) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in A Dirac set function is a probability measure.
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a set $X$, let $x_0\in X$, and let
$\delta_{x_0}$ be the Dirac probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For every
nonnegative $\mathcal A$-measurable $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_X f\,d\delta_{x_0}=f(x_0).$$

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set and let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ be probability vectors, so their coordinates are nonnegative and each vector sums to $1$. A coupling is an $m\times m$ matrix $\pi$ with $\pi_{ij}\ge0$, row sums $\sum_j\pi_{ij}=p_i$, and column sums $\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j$; write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. Writing $d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j)$, define the finite-metric 1-Wasserstein transport cost by
$$
W_1(p,q):=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d_{ij}\pi_{ij}.
$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space. Write $\mathcal B(X)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of its metric topology. A Borel probability measure on $X$ is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(X)$ with total mass one. For Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $X$, let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the set of Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on $X\times X$, with its product topology and Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A),\qquad \gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A).$$
Define
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the infimum is taken in the extended real line and $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The integrand is nonnegative and Borel: the triangle inequality and symmetry give
$$|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y'),$$
so $(x,y)\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous for the product topology; nonnegativity follows from the metric axioms.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on it, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of real-valued $\Sigma$-measurable functions that are integrable under both $P$ and $Q$. The **integral probability metric** induced by $\mathcal F$ is
$$d_{\mathcal F}(P,Q):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\int_S f\,dP-\int_S f\,dQ\right|\in[0,+\infty].$$
It is nonnegative and symmetric, and it may equal $+\infty$; no separation property is asserted for an arbitrary class $\mathcal F$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: For $t>0$, the second row sum $0$ and nonnegative entries force $\pi_{21}=\pi_{22}=0$; the first column sum $0$ then forces $\pi_{11}=0$, and the first row sum $1$ forces $\pi_{12}=1$, which also gives the required second column sum $1$. This is the unique feasible matrix, and [F3] gives finite-space cost $d(0,t)=t$. For $t=0$, the singleton probability vector has unique coupling $(1)$ and cost $0$.

By [F1], $P$ and $Q_t$ are Borel probability measures. If $\gamma$ is any coupling of $P$ and $Q_t$, then $\gamma(\{0\}\times X)=1$ and $\gamma(X\times\{t\})=1$. The complement of their intersection is contained in the union of their two null complements, so finite subadditivity from [F6] gives $\gamma(\{(0,t)\})=1$. A probability measure concentrated on the singleton $(0,t)$ equals its Dirac measure there: sets containing $(0,t)$ have mass $1$, and sets omitting it have mass $0$. The Dirac measure at $(0,t)$ has the required marginals, so it is the unique coupling. By [F2] and [F4], its cost is $d(0,t)=t$, so $W_1(P,Q_t)=t$, including $t=0$.
Every function in the specified $1$-Lipschitz class satisfies $|f(0)-f(t)|\le t$, and $f(x)=x$ belongs to the class and has $|f(0)-f(t)|=t$. By [F5], the IPM is exactly $t$.

If $t>0$, the mixture $(P+Q_t)/2$ assigns mass $1/2$ to each of $0$ and $t$. The finite sum definition gives $\operatorname{KL}(P\|(P+Q_t)/2)=\log2$ and $\operatorname{KL}(Q_t\|(P+Q_t)/2)=\log2$, so $\operatorname{JS}(P,Q_t)=\log2$. If $t=0$, the two laws agree, each KL term is $0$, and the JS value is $0$.

Under the weight bounds, the slope of $f_{a,b}(x)=abx$ has absolute value at most $c^2$. If $c>1$, the allowed choice $a=b=c$ gives slope $c^2>1$. If $0<c<1$, every allowed slope has magnitude less than $1$, so the function $x$ cannot occur. Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined). To apply The recursion theorem with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$.
